name: Pull-up and chin-up
angleNote: Pull: 0% = hanging with straight arms, 100% = chest at the bar. Load = extra weight on a belt; the body weight is always lifted. Torques per arm; drag the figure to turn it.
momentArmNote: Moment arm = the joint's 3D distance from the bar's push line through that hand (straight up); it feeds every component of that joint's torque.

strength.note: Shoulder extension (positive) and flexion (negative) peak torque per arm, taken as constant: Mayer's isometric means for men (93 and 68 Nm). Kulig et al. describe extension strength as rising then falling with the arm's angle, but give no numbers to scale it.
strength.source: Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25, Table 2 (men, dominant side, isometric); Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (shapes)

strength.note: Shoulder adduction (positive: lats, with the hands wide) and abduction (negative) peak torque per arm, taken as constant: Mayer's isometric means for men (72 and 47 Nm). Clarke et al. (64 men, via Kulig et al.) found adduction strongest with the arm out at 90–110° and nearly symmetric from 25° to 180°; the size of the change isn't given as numbers here.
strength.source: Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25, Table 2 (men, dominant side, isometric); Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (shapes)

strength.note: Shoulder external (positive) and internal (negative) rotation peak torque per arm, taken as constant: Mayer's isometric means for men (30 and 43 Nm).
strength.source: Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25, Table 2 (men, dominant side, isometric)

strength.note: Relative isometric elbow-flexion torque vs elbow flexion (0° = straight), peak about 95°: the paper's mean cubic fit, normalised, inside the measured 32–120° (held flat beyond). Measured with the upper arm raised 90° and horizontally adducted 20°, not hanging as in a standing curl. Peak per arm: the paper's male means (flexion 85 Nm, extension 77 Nm). Variants correct it for the arm being overhead and the grip (Guenzkofer et al., see each variant).
strength.source: Pinter IJ, Bobbert MF, van Soest AJ, Smeets JBJ (2010). Isometric torque–angle relationships of the elbow flexors and extensors in the transverse plane. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 20:923–931. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2010.05.001

strength.note: No muscle capacity: the elbow's sideways moment is carried mostly by ligaments and the joint surfaces, so it is shown as torque only.
strength.source: Not applicable: carried by ligaments and joint surfaces, so no muscle strength is used

muscles.name: Latissimus dorsi
muscles.note: Pulls the arm down: adduction with a wide grip, extension with a close grip. It takes the larger of the two demands.

muscles.name: Teres major
muscles.note: Works with the lats on both actions.

muscles.name: Biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis
muscles.note: Elbow flexors: work while the forearm is tilted away from the line of the pull. With the elbows under the bar (wide grip) they do little; with a close grip they do much more.

muscles.name: Posterior deltoid
muscles.note: Helps extend the arm, most near the bottom.

muscles.name: Infraspinatus, teres minor
muscles.note: External rotators of the rotator cuff: hold the upper arm from turning inwards.

muscles.name: Subscapularis
muscles.note: Internal rotator of the rotator cuff: holds the upper arm from turning outwards.

muscles.name: Lower trapezius, rhomboids
muscles.note: Pull the shoulder blades down and together. Not estimated: the model has no shoulder blade.

variants.name: Pull-up, wide grip, palms down

elbow.note: palms down (pull-up grip). Elbow-flexion strength relative to palms up with the arm at the side, by the shoulder's angle (0°, 60°, 135°) and the elbow's (0–120°), from Guenzkofer et al.'s measured table; held at the 135° values above that. Their shoulder angle is flexion (arm forwards); the arm's elevation is used for it here, also when the arm is out to the side. Palms down and overhead is the weakest combination: about 60% at 135° of shoulder flexion and 45–90° of elbow flexion. The 60°/90° value assumes a sign was lost in their table (listed as +90°, but the row is the third forearm position).
elbow.source: Guenzkofer F, Bubb H, Bengler K (2012). Maximum elbow joint torques for digital human models. Int J Human Factors Modelling and Simulation 3(2):109–132. doi:10.1504/IJHFMS.2012.051092 (Table A1: 20 young men, isometric)

variants.notes: Hands wide, palms down. The bar pushes each hand straight up with half the body's weight, and the body leans back until its centre of mass hangs under the bar. Wide hands make it mostly shoulder adduction: about as much as men's measured maximum at 75 kg, which is why pull-ups are hard. The hands move in a straight line in the trunk's frame; the shoulder joints stay put (no shoulder-blade movement).

variants.name: Chin-up, palms up

elbow.note: palms up (chin-up grip). Elbow-flexion strength relative to palms up with the arm at the side, by the shoulder's angle (0°, 60°, 135°) and the elbow's (0–120°), from Guenzkofer et al.'s measured table; held at the 135° values above that. Their shoulder angle is flexion (arm forwards); the arm's elevation is used for it here, also when the arm is out to the side. Overhead the elbow flexors are much weaker: 70% at 135° of shoulder flexion and 90° of elbow flexion.
elbow.source: Guenzkofer F, Bubb H, Bengler K (2012). Maximum elbow joint torques for digital human models. Int J Human Factors Modelling and Simulation 3(2):109–132. doi:10.1504/IJHFMS.2012.051092 (Table A1: 20 young men, isometric)

variants.notes: Hands at shoulder width, palms up: the arms come down in front, so the shoulder works in extension and the elbow flexors take a large share. Palms up, the elbow flexors are stronger than palms down, which is one reason most people find chin-ups easier. The hands move in a straight line in the trunk's frame; the shoulder joints stay put (no shoulder-blade movement).

variants.name: Neutral grip (parallel handles)

elbow.note: neutral (parallel) grip. Elbow-flexion strength relative to palms up with the arm at the side, by the shoulder's angle (0°, 60°, 135°) and the elbow's (0–120°), from Guenzkofer et al.'s measured table; held at the 135° values above that. Their shoulder angle is flexion (arm forwards); the arm's elevation is used for it here, also when the arm is out to the side.
elbow.source: Guenzkofer F, Bubb H, Bengler K (2012). Maximum elbow joint torques for digital human models. Int J Human Factors Modelling and Simulation 3(2):109–132. doi:10.1504/IJHFMS.2012.051092 (Table A1: 20 young men, isometric)

variants.notes: Palms facing each other, hands a little wider than the shoulders. The hands move in a straight line in the trunk's frame; the shoulder joints stay put (no shoulder-blade movement).

phases.name: Hang
phases.text: Arms straight overhead: the shoulders hold the body up.

phases.name: Pull
phases.text: The elbows bend most here: the elbow flexors peak, and the body starts to lean back.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Chest to the bar: the arms are back at the sides and the shoulder extensors finish the pull.

placement.label: Grip: each hand from the middle
Elbows outside (+) / inside (−) the hands, front view
